extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners (applicants/attorneys)
extracted.subtask_description: Determine whether a claim limitation invokes 35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph (means-/step-plus-function), and whether the specification discloses corresponding structure/material/acts (including computer-implemented algorithms) sufficient to support such a limitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption from phrase 'means for' or 'step for'
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim limitation is presumed to invoke 35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph when it explicitly uses the phrase 'means for' or 'step for' and includes functional language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: That presumption is overcome when the limitation further includes the structure necessary to perform the recited function. See TriMed, Inc. v. Stryker Corp., 514 F.3d 1256, 1259-60 (Fed. Cir. 2008). If applicant uses the phrase in the preamble, a §112, second paragraph rejection may be appropriate where it is unclear whether the preamble is reciting a means-plus-function limitation or merely stating intended use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption against §112(6) when phrase absent
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim limitation that does not use the phrase 'means for' or 'step for' will trigger the rebuttable presumption that 35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph does not apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a strong presumption not readily overcome (Phillips v. AWH Corp.; Lighting World v. Birchwood Lighting). It may be overcome if the limitation uses a non-structural term (a nonce word or verbal construct that is effectively a substitute for 'means for').

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-structural terms that may invoke §112(6)
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-structural terms that may invoke 35 U.S.C. 112, paragraph 6 include 'mechanism for,' 'module for,' 'device for,' 'unit for,' 'component for,' 'element for,' 'member for,' 'apparatus for,' 'machine for,' or 'system for.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The list is not exhaustive; other non-structural terms may invoke §112(6) (Welker Bearing Co.; Massachusetts Inst. of Tech.; Personalized Media). Whether such a term invokes §112(6) depends on context and whether the term denotes structure to one of ordinary skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural terms that avoid §112(6)
rubrics_metrics.description: A term that denotes structure to a person of ordinary skill in the art (even if it covers a broad class of structures) will not invoke §112(6). Examples: 'filters,' 'brakes,' 'clamp,' 'screwdriver,' 'locks,' 'circuit,' 'detent mechanism,' 'digital detector,' 'reciprocating member,' 'connector assembly,' 'perforation,' 'sealingly connected joints,' 'eyeglass hanger member.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The term need not denote a precise physical structure to avoid §112(6). Case law examples: Lighting World; Apex; CCS Fitness; Watts; Greenberg.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three‑prong test for invoking §112(6)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners will apply 35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph to a claim limitation if it meets the following 3-prong analysis: (A) the claim limitation uses the phrase 'means for' or 'step for' or a non-structural term; (B) the phrase or non-structural term is modified by functional language; and (C) the phrase or non-structural term is not modified by sufficient structure, material, or acts for achieving the specified function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply all three prongs; if all met, treat the limitation as means-/step-plus-function. If not met, explain why in the Office action. See MPEP § 2181.

rubrics_metrics.name: First prong — determining non-structural vs structural usage
rubrics_metrics.description: When the claim limitation does not include 'means for,' examiners should determine whether the presumption that §112(6) does not apply is overcome by a non-structural term (a term simply a substitute for 'means for').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if a term is broad, if persons of ordinary skill understand it as the name for the structure that performs the function, §112(6) will not apply (Lighting World; Apex; CCS Fitness; Watts). Examples of structural terms found not to invoke §112(6) are provided in MPEP. The list of non-structural terms is illustrative, not exhaustive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant options when examiner does not find invocation
rubrics_metrics.description: If the examiner has not interpreted a claim limitation as invoking 35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph and an applicant wishes it to be treated under §112(6), applicant must either: (A) amend the claim to include the phrase 'means for' or 'step for'; or (B) rebut the presumption that §112(6) does not apply by showing that the limitation is written as a function to be performed and does not recite sufficient structure, material, or acts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case authority: Watts v. XL Systems; Masco Corp. v. United States. Conversely, if applicant used 'means for' but did include structure, the examiner should explain why §112(6) is not being applied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second prong — functional modification requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The phrase 'means for' or the non-structural term must be modified by functional language — i.e., the element is set forth, at least in part, by the function it performs rather than by specific structure, material, or acts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the term 'means' is not linked to a specific function, §112(6) may not be invoked. For method claims, §112(6) is implicated only when steps-plus-function without acts are present; mere 'ing' verbs do not automatically convert steps into step-plus-function clauses. See York Prod.; Caterpillar; O.I. Corp.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third prong — absence of sufficient structure/material/acts
rubrics_metrics.description: The phrase 'means for' or the non-structural term must not be modified by sufficient structure, material, or acts for achieving the specified function; if sufficient modifying structure is recited, §112(6) does not apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples where sufficient structure removed the limitation from §112(6): 'second baffle means' with baffle structure recited; 'perforation means…for tearing' where perforation structure described. Conversely, 'spring means' was found to invoke §112(6). If a non-structural term has a structural modifier (e.g., 'detent mechanism'), §112(6) will not apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determining whether a term denotes structure — three checks
rubrics_metrics.description: To determine whether a word, term, or phrase coupled with a function denotes structure, examiners should check whether: (1) the specification provides a description sufficient to inform one of ordinary skill in the art that the term denotes structure; (2) general and subject matter specific dictionaries provide evidence that the term has achieved recognition as a noun denoting structure; and (3) the prior art provides evidence that the term has an art-recognized structure to perform the claimed function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This three-part analysis is from Ex parte Rodriguez (precedential). Use these sources to assess whether a term is structural or non-structural in context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Element-by-element application of §112(6)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is necessary to decide on an element-by-element basis whether 35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph applies; not all terms in a means-plus-function clause are limited to what is disclosed in the written description and equivalents, since §112(6) applies only to the interpretation of the means or step that performs the recited function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each claim must be independently reviewed even where process and apparatus claims use substantially similar language (O.I. Corp.). Do not assume that language in one claim governs another.

rubrics_metrics.name: Office action content when treating or not treating under §112(6)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a claim limitation meets the 3-prong analysis and is being treated under 35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph, the examiner will include a statement in the Office action that the claim limitation is being treated under §112(6). If a claim limitation uses 'means for' or 'step for' but the examiner determines that either the second or third prong is not met, the examiner must include a statement in the Office action explaining the reasons why the claim limitation is not being treated under §112(6).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transparency in the Office action is required so applicants understand the reasoning and can respond appropriately. See MPEP § 2181 subsection VI.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of §112, second paragraph rejection when unclear
rubrics_metrics.description: In the event that it is unclear whether the claim limitation falls within the scope of 35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph, a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph may be appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be alert to ambiguity that prevents a clear determination under the 3-prong test; §112 second paragraph addresses definiteness issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corresponding-structure disclosure requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The corresponding structure (or material or acts) of a means (or step)-plus-function limitation must be disclosed in the specification itself in a way that one skilled in the art will understand what structure (or material or acts) will perform the recited function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A bare statement that known techniques or methods can be used does not disclose structure for means-plus-function purposes (Biomedino). If no disclosure exists, the claim fails to satisfy §112, second paragraph. Disclosure may be explicit, implicit, or shown in drawings where appropriate (Atmel; Dossel; Vas-Cath).

rubrics_metrics.name: Implicit/inherent disclosure and drawings
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclosure of the structure may be implicit or inherent in the specification if it would have been clear to those skilled in the art what structure corresponds to the means-plus-function limitation; drawings may also provide the written description required by §112.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even where structure is not spelled out in prose, drawings or incorporated references can suffice if they make the corresponding structure clear to one skilled in the art (Atmel; Vas-Cath). However, courts emphasize that the specification itself must disclose structure — one skilled's knowledge alone is not a substitute for disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: §112(6) does not excuse compliance with §112 paragraphs 1 and 2
rubrics_metrics.description: Invocation of 35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph does not exempt an applicant from compliance with the written-description and definiteness requirements of 35 U.S.C. 112, first and second paragraphs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Means-plus-function claiming requires adequate specification disclosure of corresponding structure; failure to do so can result in §112(2) indefiniteness or written description failures (Donaldson; Knowlton).

rubrics_metrics.name: Computer-implemented means-plus-function — general vs specific functions
rubrics_metrics.description: For a computer-implemented means-plus-function claim limitation, a general purpose computer is usually sufficient as corresponding structure for performing a general computing function (e.g., 'means for storing data'), but the corresponding structure for performing a specific function must be more than simply a general purpose computer or microprocessor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the claimed function requires a specific implementation, the specification must disclose the algorithm needed to transform the general purpose computer into a special purpose computer capable of performing that specific function. Cases: Katz; Aristocrat; Finisar; WMS Gaming.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algorithm disclosure requirement for computer-implemented functions
rubrics_metrics.description: To claim a computer-implemented means-plus-function and avoid pure functional claiming, the specification must disclose the algorithm that transforms the general purpose computer into the special purpose computer designed to perform the disclosed algorithm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An algorithm may be expressed as a mathematical formula, in prose, in a flow chart, or any other understandable terms that provide sufficient structure. Applicant need not provide source code, but must disclose the algorithmic steps (Aristocrat; Finisar; WMS Gaming).

rubrics_metrics.name: Insufficiency of generic computer/software references
rubrics_metrics.description: Mere reference to a general purpose computer with appropriate programming, or simply reciting 'software' without providing detail about the programming, or referencing 'logic,' 'code,' or other undefined computer components (black boxes) will not be sufficient disclosure of corresponding structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If no corresponding algorithm is disclosed, a §112, second paragraph rejection is appropriate (Aristocrat; Blackboard; NetMoneyIN; Rodriguez). Provide concrete explanation of how the computer component performs the function rather than labeling it with generic terms.
